questions.q: What does Hyatt compare a Life Plan to?
a: A GPS that guides you and reroutes you without judgment
A map you draw once and then never change
A contract you sign with your employer
A diary that records your past achievements
questions.why: The first lesson uses the phone's GPS as a metaphor for a plan that directs you and gets you back on course.

questions.q: How much time does Hyatt say writing your Life Plan deserves?
a: An entire day away from home and work
One focused hour at your desk
A weekend at the end of every month
Fifteen minutes each morning
questions.why: The second lesson says to set aside a whole day, go somewhere new and disconnect until the plan is finished.

questions.q: Which question does Hyatt suggest you reflect on first?
a: How do I want to be remembered after I die?
How much money will I need to retire?
Who should I spend most of my time with?
Which habits should I give up first?
questions.why: The three key questions begin with your legacy, then your values, then the steps from where you are to the life you want.

questions.q: What does Hyatt recommend doing right after writing the plan?
a: Read it aloud every day for 90 days
Store it safely and revisit it once a year
Share it only with a trusted mentor
Rewrite it from scratch every week
questions.why: The third lesson says to cement the plan by reading it out loud daily for 90 days, then review it weekly and quarterly.

questions.q: What did the company's three-day planning retreat show?
a: A plan changes nothing if nobody implements it
Retreats produce better plans than individuals do
Outside consultants should write every plan
Formal plans always fail in growing companies
questions.why: The team created a detailed plan and then shelved it, which is why Hyatt calls the Life Plan a living document.
